doc.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Writing songs for Louis Jordan
summary: He wrote I'll Die Happy, I Want You to Be My Baby, and Messy Bessie for Louis Jordan.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I guess this is – what? – in the ’52 to ’54 time period? You had written Four Brothers. I guess you were doing a lot of writing during that period.

I was writing for Louis Jordan. I was writing what I call unpopular songs. But I did write one for Louis Jordan called I’ll Die Happy, which was chosen number one rhythm-and-blues song of 1957 by Cash Box on the cover.
[Hendricks sings:] “I’m a real fast liver, trouble giver, whiskey taster, and a money waster, and the old folks say I won’t live long. But I’ll die happy.”
Yes, yes, yes. And you also wrote I Want You to be My Baby?

Yes. I wrote that for Louis Jordan. He recorded that on Decca. But in those days they wanted you to get right to the vocal. Louis Jordan started playing that tune, that boogie-woogie blues riff. He blew three choruses and then sang the vocal, so of course the disc jockeys wouldn’t play it. But a lady truck driver named Lillian Briggs in Pittsburgh heard Louis’s version. She recorded it and got right to the vocal – from the introduction into the vocal. Then that sold a million.
Yeah, I wrote that for Louis.
Last night I was in Tower Records. I went to Louis Jordan’s bin, and of all things, what comes up?
No. It’s “and you call that a buddy.”
Oh. Do You Call that a Buddy? I love that. I love that song.
It’s a great song, and he used to sing it. Boy, Louis sang that thing.
Did you write that for him?
No, no. I didn’t write that. I just loved it.
I wish I had written that. That’s a great song.
